reasoning_traces.think:
The foundational tension in behavior theory lies between the apparent simplicity of actions and the deep complexity of their underlying mechanisms. Reification—treating functional relationships as if they were material objects—introduces conceptual noise that obscures causal structure. The robotic approach counters this by insisting on formal, mechanistic description rather than teleological or vitalistic ones. This aligns with modern computational modeling where behavior emerges from interactions in high-dimensional spaces. The principle of behavioral complexity implies that even simple acts involve intricate dynamical systems governed by differential equations, whose solutions may be analytically intractable but computationally simulatable. Thus, GSI employs Bayesian inference over these systems to estimate posterior distributions of behavioral states, while GSE uses kernel-based approximations to navigate state transitions efficiently. Both rely on objectivist frameworks that avoid metaphysical entanglement.
